title: Don’t Slow Down AI Development—Speed Up Benchmarking
gist: CSIS Futures Lab (Jensen and Atalan) argues the US should reject P(doom)-driven slowdowns and instead accelerate AI development while massively funding independent benchmarking via NSF, NIST public-private partnerships, university policy labs and possibly a Tobin-style token levy, and push shared evaluation standards in US-China AI diplomacy around the Trump-Xi summit.

insights.claim: Prominent AI leaders have issued high existential-risk estimates: Geoffrey Hinton put AI-caused human extinction at 10-20% within 30 years (Dec 2024), Elon Musk gave a similar estimate, and Dario Amodei put the chance of things going 'really, really badly' at 25% (Sep 2025).
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Headline risk estimates from lab leaders drive regulatory sentiment and public anxiety, a policy overhang for AI equities.

insights.claim: Frontier-lab warnings about AI catastrophe may partly be market positioning, letting companies pose as safety champions while effectively regulating themselves.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Treat lab safety rhetoric as potentially strategic (regulatory moat-building) rather than purely a risk signal.
insights.quote: the surge of fear could be clever market positioning, with companies acting like champions of safety for the simple act of regulating themselves

insights.claim: Circulating AI risk estimates lack credibility because they use differing definitions, time horizons and assumptions about safeguards, and there are no clear metrics for model or agentic risk.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Demand for standardized risk metrics creates an opening for evaluation/benchmarking vendors and standards bodies.
insights.locator: Circulating risk estimates and institutional positions

themes.theme: Industry convergence on pacing and oversight

insights.claim: Amodei's 'We Must Pace the Frontier' proposes three levels: embedded independent evaluators with employee-like access and publication rights, common safety standards and capability-triggered checkpoints among democratic labs (with narrow antitrust waivers), and verifiable international agreements including with China.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Capability-triggered checkpoints and antitrust waivers would reshape competitive dynamics among frontier labs.
insights.locator: Proposing safety measures is the right direction

insights.claim: Frontier AI leaders broadly agree on human control but differ on mechanisms: Altman backs pacing, independent audits and federal standards without waiting for legislation; Hassabis wants a federally overseen frontier-AI standards body; Microsoft requires models to accept correction and shutdown; Zuckerberg proposes board-level release oversight and early government access.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Cross-industry convergence raises odds of a federal standards regime; watch which mechanism wins as it sets compliance costs.
insights.locator: There is substantial agreement in the AI community

insights.claim: The US should speed up both AI development and independent evaluation rather than halting development or relying on company self-regulation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Signals think-tank support for pro-acceleration policy paired with evaluation spending, not moratoria.
insights.quote: the United States must speed up both AI development and the checks and balances required
insights.locator: Every news outlet has lately been seduced

insights.claim: There are no national security benchmarks for military AI, including missing standards for how model outputs align with the Laws of Armed Conflict, leaving the public in the dark about military AI risks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defense AI evaluation is an underbuilt niche likely to attract government funding.
insights.locator: AI benchmarking is the way ahead

insights.claim: Independent benchmarking is valuable only with rigorous methods, meaningful model access and continued scrutiny as capabilities change; catastrophe predictions offer little guidance on how systems behave in national security decisions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Model access rights for third-party evaluators will be a key regulatory battleground.

themes.theme: Funding mechanisms for AI safety research

insights.claim: Congress should expand AI safety research via the NSF and let NIST coordinate public-private partnerships for common benchmarks, modeled on NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation and the Trump administration's X-Labs grand challenges.
insights.speaker: CSIS
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: Watch appropriations for NIST/CAISI and NSF as indicators of federal evaluation spending.
insights.locator: The federal government can help AI development

insights.claim: The NSF's budget has been cut by over 50 percent in recent years, constraining basic AI safety research grants to universities and nonprofits.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Public research funding gap means private/foundation money and industry must fill AI evaluation needs.
insights.locator: The push to support deeper AI safety research

insights.claim: A Tobin-style tax on AI tokens could finance public-interest AI safety research and standards, alongside foundation matching grants.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A per-token levy would be a direct cost on AI inference providers; low odds but a tail policy risk to monitor.
insights.quote: even creative mechanisms such as a Tobin tax on tokens
insights.locator: The push to support deeper AI safety research

insights.claim: Universities and nonprofits should host policy labs testing AI in high-risk workflows such as national security, large-scale cyberattacks and bioterrorism, broadening evaluation beyond internal frontier-lab researchers.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Third-party evaluation ecosystem likely to grow; beneficiaries include evaluation startups and academic partners.
insights.locator: At their core, these efforts should build

insights.claim: US foreign policy should push international AI evaluation benchmarks to prevent the US-China AI arms race from becoming a security dilemma.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Shared benchmark agreements would be a de-escalation signal in US-China tech competition.
insights.locator: AI benchmarking is the way ahead

insights.claim: Trump and Xi will likely discuss AI at their upcoming summit, but neither side has appetite to slow AI progress; China's spy chief has warned the CCP of political risks from AI advances and urged more control over its development.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Expect governance talk, not slowdown commitments; AI capex race continues on both sides.
insights.quote: neither side seems primed to show much appetite for slowing down AI progress
